summary: Leveraged looping (recursive lending) repeatedly deposits collateral, borrows against it and re-deposits to multiply exposure, so net return on equity is collateral yield times leverage minus borrow rate times (leverage minus 1); the pack covers LST and stablecoin loops, venue mechanics (Kamino Multiply, eMode/elevation groups, Aave), liquidation math, depeg and rate-inversion risk, and flash-loan unwind cost across 7 research facets. Evidence status: research claims ungated (v4 evidence gate not passed); treat as leads with cited sources. Educational framing only, not financial advice; leverage can lose more than the stake.

facts.text: The 1/(1-maxLTV) ceiling is the liquidation edge, not a target. Kamino says operating at the maximum puts Current LTV exactly at the liquidation threshold and real positions need a buffer below it. Aave's health factor is collateral x weighted-average liquidation threshold / debt, and liquidation is possible below 1, so a position at LTV equal to the threshold has HF = 1.

Kamino Multiply deleverage is one atomic transaction: flash-borrow the debt token, repay debt, withdraw the freed collateral, swap collateral to the debt token via KSwap, repay the flash loan, then send the remainder to the user. SDK method getWithdrawWithLeverageIxs handles deleverage-and-withdraw; getRepayWithCollIxs handles repay-with-collateral and keeps value in the position. The worked examples use TSLAx/USDC, not an LST pair, but the docs name the same methods for all Multiply positions.

A Kamino elevation group (eMode) is a curator-defined cluster of correlated assets (stablecoins, LSTs with their underlying SOL, wrapped assets with natives). A user joins voluntarily; the program then applies the group's LTV and liquidation threshold in place of per-reserve defaults. Leaving the group, or borrowing an asset outside it, restores the per-reserve defaults.

In the finance literature 'carry' means return with prices held fixed, which is the sense in which the loop formula is a carry. Koijen, Moskowitz, Pedersen and Vrugt (Journal of Financial Economics, 2018) define an asset's carry as 'its futures return, assuming that prices stay the same' and split return into carry + E(price appreciation) + unexpected price shock. The loop formula likewise holds Y, B, L and the collateral/debt price ratio fixed, so it is a steady-state figure and not an expected return. SODAX labels its number 'Steady-state, not realised'. Kamino Multiply unwinds are one atomic transaction. In the SDK's default 'debt flash' path it flash-borrows the debt token, repays debt, withdraws collateral, swaps the collateral to the debt token through Kamino Swap (KSwap), repays the flash loan, and sends any remainder to the wallet. If any step fails (slippage beyond tolerance, insufficient liquidity), the whole transaction reverts and no state changes. The SDK also has a 'coll' variant that flash-borrows collateral first, swaps it, then repays and withdraws.

Effective stETH exit depth is a small fraction of nominal liquidity. A Lido research thread (20 February 2024) says the Curve stETH/ETH pool held about 46k ETH but only about 7k ETH of depth at 100 bps: 6,870 stETH moves the price 100 bps at amplification A=30, and a proposed A=200 would need 33,721 stETH. Cork (September 2025) says only $10-20M can exit through AMMs at once without meaningful price impact, against roughly $450M of AMM liquidity.

A manual loop is a geometric series. Each round borrows LTV times the last deposit and re-deposits it, so after n rounds total collateral is c*(1 + L + L^2 + ... + L^n) = c*(1 - L^(n+1))/(1 - L), which converges to c/(1 - L) for L < 1. Leverage after n rounds is (1 - L^(n+1))/(1 - L) and always sits below the ceiling 1/(1 - L).

The formula is a steady-state estimate, not a realised APY. SODAX says the figure is what a position earns at targetLTV if rates stay constant, and that realised APY depends on rebalancing, rate volatility and time spent off-target. The arXiv backtest reports that results depend strongly on position size and rebalancing frequency.

A per-group collateral cap of 0 is a hard stop, not 'no cap'. update_elevation_group_debt_trackers_on_borrow requires borrow_limit_against_this_collateral_in_elevation_group[group] >= the new tracked debt for every collateral reserve in the obligation, and klend-sdk drops groups whose cap is 0 from its candidate list. Kamino's reserve template shows every cap as '0' and its checklist says that without the cap 'the group has no per-asset cap'; unlimited is u64::MAX. Each collateral reserve's counter is credited with the obligation's whole group debt, so an obligation with two collateral reserve

With several collateral reserves the program's threshold is the value-weighted average: unhealthy_borrow_value is the sum of value_i x threshold_i, so adding a lower-threshold collateral to a loop lowers the blended threshold. For an LTV-exceeded liquidation the liquidator must repay the highest-borrow-factor debt and seize the lowest-liquidation-LTV collateral first (errors LiquidationBorrowFactorPriority and LiquidationLowestLiquidationLtvPriority). Inside an eMode group the group threshold applies to every collateral, so no blend arises.

A market supports at most 32 elevation groups (IDs 1-32; 0 means no group). Per the docs, a single reserve can opt into up to 20 groups, and group parameters only apply to reserves that list the group ID in their own elevation_groups array.

Group configuration is not exposed through the REST API; a curator sets it through the SDK or Kamino CLI. Setting allow_new_loans to 0 pauses new borrows in a group while existing positions keep their relaxed parameters and can still repay and exit.

Kamino's eMode is the elevation group. One lending market stores up to 32 groups (ids 1-32; id 0 means no group). Each group sets ltv_pct, liquidation_threshold_pct, max_liquidation_bonus_bps, allow_new_loans, max_reserves_as_collateral and exactly one debt_reserve.

Venue fee schedules at unwind differ. Kamino Swap, which the docs name as the execution layer for all Multiply flash-loan swaps (open, adjust and close), charges no platform fee; costs are Solana transaction fees plus any spread inside the underlying routes. It is a meta-aggregator that queries 15 or more routers in parallel (Jupiter/Metis, DFlow, OKX, Settler, LI.FI, OpenOcean, Titan and others) and takes the best output. Where Aave's interface swaps through CoW Protocol, debt swaps carry 0 bps and other swap operations carry 15 bps between correlated assets (the docs' example is ETH/wstETH)

If a loop earns less than its headline Net, check four leaks in this order. (1) Off-target leverage: SODAX says a position with ltv below targetLTV 'is under-leveraged and earns less than the headline number'. (2) Stale or smoothed Y: SODAX's lsdStaking is DefiLlama's trailing yield, 'typically a 7- to 30-day window', and Jito's MEV component 'fluctuate[s] significantly between epochs'. (3) The position's own size: in the arXiv backtest (Morpho wstETH/WETH, 2025-01-01 to 2025-04-01, leverage capped at 5, zero fees) a $10k position earned 6.2% APY with hourly rebalancing and a $10m position 3.7

Reports use 'carry' for three different spreads, and each moves a different part of the loop. (1) Loop carry is sUSDe yield minus the Aave stablecoin borrow APY: Sentora wrote that USDT/USDC borrow rates 'exceed sUSDe yield by ~2.0%/1.5%, making carry negative', and CryptoSlate described a 'negative carry before incentives, transaction costs, and other frictions'. (2) Ethena's hedge carry: the New York Fed says the spread between USDe's yield and the ether staking yield 'turned negative' on 2025-10-10, 'meaning the cost of maintaining the short futures exceeded the return from staking', and th

For an LST loop, Y is exchange-rate drift measured in the debt asset, not a pool distribution. Jito defines 'Exchange Rate = Total Pool Lamports / Pool Token Supply', pays rewards at epoch boundaries (about every 2 days), and says MEV rewards 'fluctuate significantly between epochs'. Kamino prices an LST as SOL_staked / LST_minted, a ratio that 'increases monotonically each epoch'. SODAX makes the same point for ETH LSDs: the staking yield 'doesn't show in currentLiquidityRate. It just accrues to the token-price', so SODAX adds it to the lending supply APR. Y therefore arrives in epoch-sized s

Kamino has two different unwind operations. getWithdrawWithLeverageIxs ('deleverage and withdraw') sells collateral, repays part of the debt and pays the rest to the wallet; the position shrinks but keeps its LTV, so leverage is unchanged. getRepayWithCollIxs ('repay with collateral') sells collateral to repay debt while the remaining value stays in the position, so LTV and leverage fall. The Kamino UI offers one-click equivalents (Adjust Leverage in Multiply, Repay With Collateral in the Loan Dashboard) and a manual withdraw, swap, repay route.

Automation venues replace manual loops with flash-loan builds. Contango, DeFi Saver and Instadapp do it on Aave, Morpho and Spark (Contango says Instadapp and DeFi Saver did so from 2019), and Kamino Multiply does it on Solana. Cork lists Morpho Blue isolated markets, Aave eMode correlated-asset categories and Gearbox credit accounts as designs that contain contagion to one pair or account. All four sources are vendor material.

Y differs in durability by source, and that sets how much of L×Y a planner can rely on. Kamino separates structural yield (staking 'exists whether or not anyone is using Multiply') from fee-driven yield (JLP) and credit-market yield (RWAs), 'both of which can compress or disappear'. Ethena's sUSDe reward is funding and basis income that 'will vary considerably (even day to day)' and can be zero. Chaos Labs shows part of the appeal of sUSDe loops is Ethena points. A loop sized on a funding or incentive yield carries a Y that can fall to zero while B stays positive.

Loop net return on equity is Net = Y×L − B×(L−1), with L = total collateral / equity, Y = collateral yield, B = borrow rate. Kamino documents it as 'Net APY = (Collateral Yield × Leverage) − (Borrow Rate × (Leverage − 1))'. Curvance's 2x worked example uses the same structure: collateral income on total collateral minus borrow cost on total debt.

A looped position's return on equity is Net = Y×L − B×(L−1), where Y is the collateral yield, B the borrow rate and L = total collateral ÷ equity. Kamino documents 'Net APY = (Collateral Yield × Leverage) − (Borrow Rate × (Leverage − 1))'. Jupiter Lend documents 'APY = Supply APY × leverage − Borrow APY × (leverage − 1)' and says the figure applies to net value (collateral minus debt), not the total position. Curvance's 2× example ($20,000 collateral at 7% minus $10,000 debt at 4% = $1,000 on $10,000 equity, 10%) has the same structure.

Observed leverage sits well below the ceiling. Baude et al. cap working leverage at 5x although their Morpho wstETH/WETH markets have LLTV 94.5% and 96.5% (ceilings 18.2x and 28.6x), and they split any position into an unleveraged part x0 = x(lmax-l)/(lmax-1) plus a part at the cap x1 = x(l-1)/(lmax-1). IFCA finds most users keep leverage well below the protocol maximum and notes that, at 80% LTV, practical recursion stops short of 5x once gas is counted.

Kamino's one explicit cost outside the Net APY formula is a flash loan fee of 0.001% per transaction (leverage-concepts page). The formula itself contains only Y, B and L, so opening and unwinding costs must be added separately.
Kamino Swap is the execution layer for all Multiply flash-loan swaps (open, adjust, close) and uses multi-DEX routing to get the best output.

B is a deterministic function of pool utilization U. Aave V3 documents a two-slope curve: R = R_base + R_slope1 × U/U_optimal for U ≤ U_optimal, and R_base + R_slope1 + R_slope2 × (U−U_optimal)/(1−U_optimal) above it. Kamino says its borrow rates 'are variable and adjust based on market utilization' and that 'a positive yield spread today can flip negative during high-utilization periods without any action on your part'. LIQUIDATION_CHECKS contains only PRICE_LOADED, PRICE_AGE_CHECKED and PRICE_USAGE_ALLOWED (0b100011, 35), while borrow-side checks such as check_borrow_possible and check_obligation_fully_refreshed_and_not_null use ALL_CHECKS (0b111111, 63). assert_obligation_liquidatable requires only LIQUIDATION_CHECKS on both reserves and the obligation. On 2026-11-06 all 15 Jupiter Lend vaults that borrow SOL listed borrowRate 494. Jupiter's liquidity-layer docs divide rates by 100 to get a percentage, so 494 reads as 4.94%. The same vaults show borrowFee 0, borrowRateMagnifier 0 and empty rewards lists, and Jupiter's docs say the protocol adds no fee on top of interest. DefiLlama's Jupiter Lend WSOL supply rate (3.73%) sits below that borrow rate, as expected. The unit applies the liquidity-layer convention to the vault field, which Jupiter does not state for the vault endpoint.

Kamino values SOL LST collateral at the stake-pool exchange rate, not the market price. A temporary market depeg does not change the position's LTV or cause liquidation. Inference: a looper who must exit during a depeg still sells the LST at the discounted market price through the swap, so the depeg is realised as unwind slippage even though no liquidation fires.

Deleveraging a stETH loop by swapping stETH on Curve adds sell pressure that can deepen the collateral discount and trigger further liquidations. Xiong et al. identify 442 leverage-staking positions over 963 days (537,123 ETH, about USD 877M) and their stress tests show liquidation and deleveraging selling cascading to other positions. Galaxy documents the same feedback in July 2025, where LST/LRT prices fell further below par under forced deleveraging.

Deleveraging itself sells the collateral. In the 10 days after the Terra crash (8-18 May 2022), arXiv:2401.08610 counts 13 users unwinding direct and 5 unwinding indirect stETH leverage positions, repaying 74,983.6 and 61,085.5 ETH of debt (about 136,069 ETH) by swapping stETH to ETH on Curve. The authors note that this selling pressure can deepen the stETH decline even when the user avoids liquidation. Nansen (via Decrypt) reports that Celsius and 3AC each withdrew 50,000 stETH from Aave on 8-9 June 2022 and moved it to FTX, and that Terra contagion was the main reason stETH left its 1:1 rati

Kamino's docs say the amount of LSTs deposited across Solana DeFi far outweighs the liquidity in DEX pools, so moderate selling can cause a temporary market depeg; they name large DEX sell orders and Solana's roughly 2-day epoch unstaking delay as causes of dislocation. Inference: exit capacity for SOL LST loops is DEX depth plus whatever instant-unstake liquidity exists (for example the Sanctum Infinity reserve), not the headline supply of the LST.

B and L feed back on each other, so at market scale the formula's inputs are not independent. Chaos Labs (Aave governance, 2025-08-02) describes loopers who borrow stables to mint USDe, convert it to sUSDe or PTs 'and repeat the cycle', and says 'When the borrowing cost on Aave exceeds the net reward from sUSDe, these positions become unprofitable, triggering exits.' With $800 million of USDe/stable debt and $550 million of sUSDe/stable debt outstanding, it estimates the unwind 'could return up to $1.3 billion in stablecoins to the protocol', easing utilisation. The destabilising side is debt

A debt-side stablecoin depeg matters only if the venue marks it. Jupiter Lend values dollar-stablecoin debt (USDC, USDT, USDG, USDS, JupUSD, PYUSD) at exactly $1 with no price feed, so a stablecoin depeg neither triggers nor prevents liquidation there (EURC debt uses a EUR/USD feed). Kamino instead applies price bands that reject stablecoin prices outside an expected range. Collateral-side stablecoin depegs and rate inversion remain risks for stable loops.

Kamino prices LSTs (JitoSOL, mSOL, bSOL) by stake rate (SOL_staked / LST_minted) read from the on-chain stake pool account, not by DEX price, so a temporary market depeg neither changes position health nor triggers liquidation. The same design exposes positions to genuine backing impairment such as a staking-protocol exploit, which lowers the stake rate.

The klend program (master branch, read 2026-11-06) tests liquidation on borrow-factor-adjusted debt against a value-weighted threshold. refresh_obligation_deposits adds each deposit's market value times its liquidation_threshold_pct to unhealthy_borrow_value, and uses the elevation-group threshold for every deposit when the obligation is in an eMode group. refresh_obligation_borrows adds each debt's market value times its borrow factor, which Reserve::borrow_factor_f fixes at 1 inside an elevation group. The swapAndRepay variant (no flash loan) takes collateralAmount as the maximum collateral swapped and debtRepayAmount as the amount to repay, an exact-out cap, so slippage costs extra collateral up to the cap. Incentive-driven carry can disappear without a price move. Curvance's example shows a loop moving from positive to negative carry when a temporary token-reward campaign ends, so Y should be split into organic yield and rewards.

Kamino's 'E-Mode caps' page describes per-pair debt limits for single-collateral, single-debt positions, entered automatically. The program has no separate pair-cap object; the mechanism that fits the description is an elevation group with max_reserves_as_collateral = 1 plus the collateral reserve's borrow_limit_against_this_collateral_in_elevation_group. The SOL/BTC Market has seven such single-collateral groups (ids 1 and 3-8), some at the reserve's own LTV (SOL to PYUSD 74/80), with caps of 0 (closed), finite (cbBTC to SOL) or u64::MAX (unlimited, for example USDT to USDC). Leverage as an equity multiplier (C*Pc / (C*Pc - D*Pd)) measures balance-sheet amplification, not net price exposure. If collateral and debt are the same asset or highly correlated, net delta can be small even when measured leverage is high (IFCA). Kamino makes the point for SOL liquid staking loops: both legs are SOL-denominated, so LTV does not move with SOL's USD price; what moves it is the LST/SOL exchange rate and the gap between staking yield and the SOL borrow rate.

Two flash-loan shapes exist for a Kamino unwind, and the SDK default is not the one Jupiter Lend uses. In klend-sdk 13.0.3 (commit 6a26d6f, 20 Oct 2026), getWithdrawWithLeverageIxs builds the debt-flash shape unless the caller passes flashBorrowType 'coll'. Debt-flash: flash-borrow the debt token, repay debt and withdraw collateral, swap collateral to debt, repay the flash loan. Coll-flash: flash-borrow the collateral token, swap it to the debt token, repay debt, withdraw collateral, and repay the flash loan from that withdrawal. A second builder flash-borrows the debt token first (swap, then deposit and borrow, then repay). Kamino's docs give a simplified seven-step order with the swap before the deposit. Aave V3 computes Health Factor as the sum over collateral assets of (collateral value in base currency x that asset's liquidation threshold) divided by total debt in base currency. When the user is in an E-mode category that covers the asset, the E-mode liquidation threshold replaces the reserve's threshold (GenericLogic.calculateUserAccountData). Aave's help page gives the same formula with a weighted-average threshold and says a health factor below 1 allows liquidation. The threshold is set per collateral asset by governance.

Kamino also uses the term E-Mode for per-pair borrow caps: a position with exactly one collateral and one debt asset matching a configured pair (e.g. SOL/USDC $50M, wBTC/USDC $30M, JUP/USDC $5M) gets that pair's cap automatically, and multi-asset positions fall back to pool-wide caps. This is a cap mechanism on top of the elevation-group LTV override, and the two uses of the word are easy to conflate.

Setting allow_new_loans = 0 stops new entries and new borrows in a group. In klend, withdrawing collateral while debt is outstanding also fails for a position in a paused group (ElevationGroupNewLoansDisabled: 'Elevation group does not accept any new loans or any new borrows/withdrawals'). Kamino docs say only that existing positions 'can repay and exit'. On 2026-11-06 Jito Market group 3 (kySOL collateral, JitoSOL debt) was paused this way. I did not test the Multiply close or adjust flow against a paused group.

Leverage multiplies the spread, so a loop only pays when collateral yield exceeds the borrow rate. A small negative spread becomes a larger annualized loss at high leverage, and variable borrow rates can rise above the supply side.

The SDK uses slippagePct to oversize what it sells, not only as a minimum-out cap. On a full close paid out in the collateral token it swaps flashRepay x (1 + slippagePct/100) / priceCollToDebt of collateral and expects debt-token output of swapIn x price / (1 + slippagePct/100). When reducing leverage in place, the adjust path withdraws |change in deposit| x (1 + slippagePct/100) x (flash repay amount / repay amount), which includes the flash fee. In the mSOL episode the lending venues' oracle choice decided who was liquidated. Marginfi priced assets at market, using a one-hour exponential moving average per Solana Compass, and said its liquidations fairly reflected market operations. Solend priced mSOL off the SOL oracle and said it does not treat an LST depeg as a liquidation trigger. SolanaFloor is a Jito Network subsidiary, and Solana Compass labels its write-up AI-generated, so treat these details as secondary.

Despite the 0.931 low, the Imperial College study found only 18 Aave V2 liquidations of stETH-collateral/ETH-debt positions between 2020-12-17 and 2023-08-07. Of those, 7 were direct leverage-staking positions and 2 were indirect. The authors attribute the low count to stETH's modest price decline. This scopes the 'depeg causes mass liquidation' headline to the 2022 episode, since a deeper depeg is untested.

Liquidation uses a looser price check than borrowing, so the effective liquidation price follows spot. klend defines ALL_CHECKS as all six PriceStatusFlags (price loaded, price age, TWAP, TWAP age, heuristic or price-band check, usage allowed) and LIQUIDATION_CHECKS as only price loaded, price age and usage allowed. get_validated_price clears the TWAP or heuristic flag when that check fails but still returns the price, and refresh_reserve stores it. New borrows, and withdrawing collateral while holding debt, require ALL_CHECKS. A spot price outside the TWAP tolerance therefore blocks those act

In the Kamino SDK flow, slippagePct also sizes the flash loan so that the worst-case swap fill still covers the repayment. The swap quote's priceAInB must be the mid price (before slippage). Passing a minimum-out price counts slippage twice and sizes the position wrong. Slippage also absorbs the gap between the best quoted route and the route actually sent.

Solana transaction size limits constrain which swap route a deleverage can use. Kamino's examples compress each KSwap route candidate with address lookup tables and send the first candidate that fits, sorted by best output. The best-output route often does not fit; in the docs' testing only one or two of five to ten routes did. The executed route can therefore be worse than the best quote, and the example code does not retry or fall back when no route fits.

A manual loop is a geometric series. Each round borrows LTV times the last deposit and re-deposits it, so total collateral is c(1 + L + L^2 + ...), which converges to c/(1-L) because L < 1. After n loops leverage is (1 - LTV^(n+1))/(1 - LTV).

borrow_limit_outside_elevation_group limits how much of the reserve itself can be borrowed outside any group: the program compares reserve.borrowed_amount_outside_elevation_group with it when sizing and checking borrows of that reserve. Kamino's docs describe it as a cap on borrows 'against this asset as collateral' outside a group. OtterSec's March 2026 report uses the code's meaning ('non-eMode debt'). A curator who sets it on a collateral reserve expecting a collateral-side cap will not get one.

For LST loops the cost of changing leverage is asymmetric. Baude et al. set the cost of minting wstETH from WETH at zero and the cost of selling at a couple of basis points plus a variable Lido redemption delay. With a 1 bp sell fee, hourly and daily rebalanced loops underperformed plain staking beyond roughly $1m and $3m of capital respectively, while a rule that rebalances only when the expected yield gain exceeds 20 bp still beat staking at $10m.

The klend-sdk reports two LTV definitions. KaminoObligation.refreshedStats.loanToValue and .liquidationLtv are for UI display: their denominators sum only deposits whose reserve LTV or liquidation LTV is above zero. obligation.loanToValue() and obligation.liquidationLtv() follow the smart contract and divide by all deposits. The two agree for a single-collateral loop but can differ when an obligation also holds a zero-LTV deposit, so compute distance to liquidation from borrowLiquidationLimit / userTotalBorrowBorrowFactorAdjusted or the contract-style methods.

Inference: Kamino's stake-rate oracle stops a market depeg from raising LTV or triggering liquidation, but an atomic unwind must sell the LST at the market price, so the discount is paid on exit. Kamino's own example has JitoSOL at 0.95 SOL on a DEX while valued at a 1.02 SOL stake rate (about 7%). A full close works only while proceeds still cover the debt, so the tolerable market discount is roughly 1 minus current LTV: about 10% at the 90% JitoSOL/SOL eMode LTV and about 13% at ~87%, before fees and the slippage tolerance. Borrow rates are a function of pool utilization on a kinked curve, so a positive carry can turn negative with no action by the borrower. Kamino's rate model is poly-linear: rates rise gradually below a target utilization and steeply above it (its illustrative stablecoin curve runs from 5% at 80% utilization to 150% at 95%; typical targets for major assets such as SOL and ETH are 60-75%). Kamino's Multiply docs say a positive spread can flip negative in high-utilization periods and that a negative spread worsens with leverage, with no floor. Kamino's Liquidation Analysis Suite in the Multiply interface simulates time-to-liquidation under borrow-rate scenarios, shows break-even leverage and yield, and runs historical backtests. Jupiter Lend shows each vault's oracle source type (market price, redemption rate or exchange price) in the app, and applies different limits to user operations (prices no older than 600 s, 2% Pyth confidence) and liquidations (7,200 s, 4%). Independent data on eMode leverage at another lender: Galaxy Research's snapshot of Aave V3 Core (block 24,932,111, 2026-04-22) found eMode loans were 58.84% of outstanding debt at an 89.4% debt/collateral ratio, with debt-weighted LTV about 90%, health factor about 1.05 and debt/equity about 10.4. weETH made up about 48% of eMode collateral, and a 10% weETH depeg would leave about $2.47B of debt against about $2.42B of collateral. Galaxy says its stressed health-factor grid is not a liquidation simulation.

For non-correlated loops, price alone triggers liquidation. In JLP/USDC Multiply the collateral can fall in USD while the debt stays flat, which raises LTV directly; Kamino's eMode does not apply, capping leverage near 3.2x at 67%. RWA/stablecoin loops (e.g. PRIME/PYUSD) have both sides dollar-denominated, so liquidation comes from a negative spread or from a redemption-liquidity problem, not from crypto prices.

Time to liquidation under negative carry (derived here). With flat dollar prices and both legs in SOL, LTV(t) = LTV0 * exp((b - y) * t), where b is the SOL borrow rate and y the LST yield. Liquidation arrives at t = ln(LiqLTV/LTV0) / (b - y). The drift rate b - y does not depend on leverage; leverage only sets LTV0 = 1 - 1/L and so the size of the cushion. At L = 8 and 90% liquidation LTV, spreads of -1%, -3% and -5% give about 2.8 years, 343 days and 206 days; a -40% spread gives about 26 days. At L = 5 and 90%, a -3% spread gives about 3.9 years. Two governance parameters bound a loop. Max LTV limits borrowing when debt is opened or added; the liquidation threshold (LT) sets where health factor HF = collateral x LT / debt falls below 1. A position at the opening cap has HF = LT/LTV, so the cushion is thin: LlamaRisk's review of Aave's sUSDe E-Mode (90% LTV, 92% LT) calls the 2% gap a buffer that must cover USDe discounts. Aave says no health factor is universally safe and lower values can suit correlated assets. Sizing a loop from the borrow LTV alone overstates how much room it has.

A loop is not static. With collateral and debt in one numeraire, LTV drifts as LTV(t) = LTV0 * exp((b - s) t), where b is the borrow rate and s the collateral yield (derived; constant rates, no rebalancing). A loop opened at 90% LTV against a 92% LT with a 1-point negative spread reaches the threshold in about ln(0.92/0.90)/0.01 = 2.2 years; at a 5-point negative spread, about 5 months. Galaxy names borrow cost above collateral yield as one of two e-mode liquidation paths (the other is a depeg), and Kamino says a persistently negative spread makes LTV drift upward.

Loop algebra (derived here; every published example below reproduces it). With equity E, leverage L, collateral L*E and debt (L-1)*E, opening LTV is 1 - 1/L and maximum leverage is 1/(1 - MaxLTV). The collateral-to-debt price ratio can fall by 1 - BF*(1 - 1/L)/LiqLTV before liquidation (BF = borrow factor, 1.0 if none). On Aave the same bound is 1 - 1/HF, and the leverage available at a given HF is L = 1/(1 - LT/HF). Reproductions: Kamino's worked example (70% LTV, 80% liquidation LTV) gives 12.5%; Xiong et al. Multiply opens a position atomically: the user picks a deposit and target leverage, the protocol flash-borrows the extra funds, Kamino Swap converts everything into the target asset (e.g. SOL to JitoSOL), the full amount is deposited as collateral, the underlying (SOL) is borrowed against it, and that borrow repays the flash loan. Multiply opens, adjusts and closes a leveraged position in one atomic transaction built on a klend flash loan (0.001% fee on each open, adjust or close). Interest accrual moves the liquidation price while the position is open. Kamino's example is a $7,000 USDC debt at a 10% borrow rate with flat prices, which drifts from 70% LTV to 77% over 12 months. A static liquidation price quoted at entry is therefore stale after entry.

This is derived by algebra, not quoted from a source. Aave's own example checks the identity: $10,000 of ETH at 80% LT with $6,000 debt has equity $4,000, l = 2.5 and HF = 1.333. Leverage is collateral value divided by equity, with equity = collateral - debt. A position with equity x at leverage l holds collateral x*l and debt x*(l-1), so LTV (debt/collateral) = 1 - 1/l and l = 1/(1 - LTV). At 2x the debt equals the equity (LTV 50%); at 3x the debt is twice the equity (LTV 66.7%). Jupiter Lend's 2x SOL example fits: 20 SOL of collateral worth $4,000 against $2,000 of debt. Jupiter also states that Net APY is measured on net value (collateral minus debt), not on total collateral.

A flash loan builds the same position in one transaction. For equity c0 and target leverage l, flash-borrow F = (l-1)*c0 of the debt asset, swap it into collateral, deposit c0 + F, borrow F against the deposit and repay the flash loan. Feasibility needs F/(c0+F) <= L, which gives k = l-1 <= L/(1-L): the same ceiling as infinite loops. Contango's example is 0.2 ETH of margin for 1 ETH of exposure (5x): flash-borrow 800 DAI, buy 0.8 ETH, lend 1 ETH, borrow 800 DAI, repay. Kamino and Morpho document the same flow, and every step reverts together if any step fails.

Kamino borrow rates are variable and set by pool utilization, so a positive spread can flip negative during high-utilization periods with no action by the position holder. Kamino's worked example of a negative spread is 3x leverage, 6% collateral yield and 8% borrow rate.

Stake-pool rate oracles are not dependency-free. Kamino reads the rate directly from each LST's on-chain stake pool account with no off-chain dependency or oracle delay. Jupiter Lend reads the same kind of rate but rejects it if the pool has not been updated in the current epoch or if a deposit or withdrawal fee exceeds 0.5%, and it limits market-feed age to 10 minutes for user operations and 2 hours for liquidations. Before relying on a venue in a stress, check what it does when the rate is rejected or stale.

Leverage is collateral over equity: l = C/(C-D), so C = l*E and D = (l-1)*E, and LTV = D/C = 1 - 1/l. The loop formula is the textbook financial-leverage identity, not a DeFi invention. The CFA Level I leveraged-return formula is R_L = R_P + (V_B/V_E)(R_P − r_D), and V_B/V_E (debt ÷ equity) equals L−1. The CFA worked example is a $250,000 portfolio, 40% debt-financed at 6%, with a 9% portfolio return ($100,000 debt, $150,000 equity), and it gives 11%. The Net formula with L = 5/3, Y = 9% and B = 6% also gives 11.0%. What DeFi changes is the behaviour of the inputs: B is variable and tied to pool utilisation, and Y can be a floating or incentive-paid yield.

Leverage is collateral divided by equity (net equity = collateral - debt). With LTV defined as debt/collateral this equals 1/(1-LTV), so the maximum leverage a market allows is 1/(1-maxLTV): 75% LTV gives 4x, 80% gives 5x, 90% gives 10x.

The cost of a liquidation round scales with leverage. Debt is (L - 1) x E, so a round that repays a share phi of debt at bonus b costs phi x (L - 1) x b of equity. At a 10% close factor a 10x loop pays 0.9% of equity per round at a 1% bonus, and at most 2.25% at the 2.5% maximum feasible bonus for a 95% threshold; a 12.5x loop pays 1.15% and at most 2.9% (derived here).

Baude, Danos and El Khalloufi show that a position with equity x at leverage l splits into an unleveraged part x0 = x*(lmax - l)/(lmax - 1) and a part at the cap x1 = x*(l - 1)/(lmax - 1): equity x at 3x with a 5x cap is half unleveraged and half at 5x. A market depeg and a fundamental depeg need different responses. A market depeg (DEX price below the stake-rate value, backing intact) comes from a liquidity imbalance or a confidence crisis and is normally closed by arbitrage. A fundamental depeg (the pool's SOL is drained or impaired) lowers the stake rate itself and can be permanent. Kamino rates a liquidity imbalance 'Low - temporary', a confidence crisis 'Medium - typically temporary', reserve depletion 'High - can be permanent' and a smart-contract exploit 'Critical - instant and total'. Manual looping is slow and exposed between steps. Kamino counts 8-10 separate transactions, each exposed to price and rate moves, against one atomic transaction with a single consolidated slippage check; Spark says one-click tools replace '30+ manual transactions'; IFCA notes extra recursion stops being worthwhile quickly 'especially when gas costs are factored in'. At 9%, a mass exit of 25% of stake through native unstaking would take at least three epochs (derived). The mainnet activation epoch was not found.

For one collateral asset with liquidation threshold LT, health factor = collateral*LT/debt = LT/LTV, so the leverage that gives a target health factor is L = 1/(1 - LT/HF) = HF/(HF - LT). Aave's help-page example (80% threshold, $10,000 collateral, $6,000 debt) gives HF 1.333 = 0.80/0.60, an equity multiplier of 2.5x. A flash loan builds the position in one transaction instead of n rounds. Borrow F = k*c0 (k = extra multiple of initial collateral c0), swap into collateral, deposit, borrow against the total, repay the flash loan. The borrow constraint B/C = k/(k+1) <= L gives k <= L/(1-L), so total collateral is at most c0/(1-L), the same ceiling as the infinite loop.

Scoping the July 2025 episode: Galaxy concludes that ETH staking architecture 'operated as intended', calls the queue a feature rather than a bug, and notes that new staking demand nearly offset the exits, so the stress fell on secondary-market discounts and wait times for loopers rather than on protocol solvency. Never remove a group id from a reserve that has open obligations. Two independent audits found it: OtterSec OS-KAMI-ADV-00 (high, August-September 2023) and RX Security finding 06 (medium, July 2023). refresh_obligation then fails with InconsistentElevationGroup, so owners cannot repay and liquidators cannot liquidate, which can leave bad debt. Both were fixed (OtterSec: PR#110) by adding the allow_new_loans pause flag instead of removing groups. Kamino's docs prescribe the same: set allow_new_loans to 0 to pause a group.

Baude, Danos and El Khalloufi (arXiv 2601.14005, 20 Jan 2026) show any leveraged position splits into an unleveraged staking part plus a part at a maximum leverage cap. They cap l at 5 in their examples rather than the theoretical maximum; a max LTV of 0.945 or higher implies a ceiling above 18x.

Derived here from the finite-n formula (the cited sources give the formula, not this table): the rounds needed to reach 90% of the ceiling grow quickly with LTV. It takes 8 rounds at 75% LTV, 10 at 80%, 21 at 90%, 31 at 93% and 44 at 95%. This is why high-LTV loops are built atomically rather than round by round; Kamino puts manual looping at 8-10 transactions and Spark at 30+.

A common shortcut multiplies the whole spread by total leverage and understates the result by exactly B. Spark's glossary writes 'Effective Yield = (Supply APY + Reward APY - Borrow APY) × Leverage' and works a 3× example (4.0% supply, 2.0% rewards, 3.5% borrow) as 2.5% × 3 = 7.5%. The Kamino/Jupiter form gives 3×6.0% − 2×3.5% = 11.0%. The shortcut charges borrow interest on L units instead of L−1 (derived comparison).

Jupiter's JLP Loans liquidate the whole position rather than a fraction, per forum participants who contrast it with the partial liquidations on Kamino and Jupiter Lend, so the threshold math marks a full close there. On 2025-10-09 Chaos Labs proposed raising maintenance margin from 80% to 90%, raising liquidation margin from 86% to 95% and cutting the liquidation fee from 6% to 2%. The thread does not show whether the proposal was adopted.

marginfi frames the same condition as a difference rather than a ratio: maintenance health = weighted assets - weighted liabilities, liquidatable when it is below zero, and its classic liquidator restores health only to zero, per MadeOnSol's reading of marginfi's documentation (the marginfi docs page returned HTTP 403 and was not read). For one asset pair this is the LTV test with asset and liability weights in place of a threshold: liquidatable when LTV >= asset weight / liability weight (derived here).

Threshold-liquidation math does not describe every lender. Curve's LLAMMA converts collateral gradually inside a price band instead of liquidating at one price; its founder reports that in the 2025-10-10 crash 118 positions were liquidated ($30.34M of $235M debt) and about 22% of positions near full liquidation were saved. This is the founder's own account of his protocol.

Native Solana unstaking limits how fast arbitrage can close an LST discount. Kamino gives about 2 days (epoch-based); Sanctum says 2-3 days. CoinDesk's 2022 report describes the same trade-off: wait until the epoch ends, or sell at a discount. Instant exits depend on DEX or pool liquidity, so Sanctum says liquidity depth decides how severe a depeg gets.

Inference, not stated by Kamino: no depeg liquidation does not mean no depeg cost. A looper who must exit during a market depeg sells the LST at the DEX price, so the discount and the price impact are realised in the swap even though the oracle never marked the position down. In calm markets the measured baseline is already 6.6 bps for jitoSOL, and the gap to the stake rate widens with size. Waiting for native unstaking (about two days on Solana, per Kamino's depeg page) avoids the discount but not the carry cost of holding the loop meanwhile.

Market-priced loops are reflexive. Kamino's LST-oracle page describes the chain: a depeg lowers collateral value, liquidations sell more of the LST, and the discount deepens. The Imperial College simulation measured the effect for stETH. Galaxy saw a voluntary version in July 2025: as borrow rates rose, deleveraging users sold or unstaked LSTs and the LST/LRT discount widened. Venue oracle design therefore decides whether the chain can start at all.

On 10 October 2025 (Sanctum debrief dated 29 October 2025), Sanctum reports all unstaked SOL inside INF was depleted serving demand, and it unstaked nearly 300,000 SOL from INF to add liquidity. SOL borrow rates rose sharply, Multiply holders saw negative APY, and Sanctum asked Jupiter Lend to raise INF's Multiply caps. The post names only bnSOL as depegged, states no depeg size, and does not mention slippage.

Sanctum's 29 October 2025 debrief (self-published, interested party): a surge in demand for unstaked SOL over about 24 hours pushed SOL borrow rates sharply higher and Multiply holders saw negative APY. Max-borrow LTV and liquidation threshold are separate, governance-set parameters that vary by market and change over time. Aave defines LTV as 'the maximum amount that can be borrowed relative to the collateral's value' and the liquidation threshold as 'the collateral ratio at which a position can be liquidated' (health factor below 1). Kamino elevation groups carry ltv_pct and liquidation_threshold_pct, which must be >= ltv_pct. Jupiter Lend says positions must stay under the vault's maximum LTV, 'which is below the Liquidation Threshold'.

In a Kamino Multiply LST loop, Net APY = Collateral Yield + Yield Spread x (Leverage - 1), where Yield Spread = collateral yield minus borrow rate. A negative spread grows more negative with leverage, and Kamino states there is no floor.

Gauntlet's April 2023 Aave method for LST eMode caps the tolerated LST/base divergence at 1 - liquidation threshold, requires liquidation slippage below the liquidation bonus, and sizes supply caps from liquidity after a halving. Its first rollout recommended one shared LST pool, with no extra buffer between the maximum historical depeg and the liquidation threshold.

Stress tests in the same study found that leverage staking amplifies cascading liquidations under a severe stETH devaluation. Liquidations and the leveraged users' own deleveraging add selling pressure on stETH, which deepens the devaluation and spreads liquidation to ordinary (non-leveraged) positions. Kamino's LST-oracle page describes the same loop for market-price oracles.

The Imperial College study counted only 18 Aave V2 liquidations of stETH-collateral, ETH-debt positions from 2020-12-17 to 2023-08-07; 7 were direct leverage-staking positions and 2 were indirect. It ties the low count to stETH's modest price decline (low 0.931). The study also records voluntary deleveraging: 13 direct and 5 indirect users repaid 74,983.6 ETH and 61,085.5 ETH, about 136,069 ETH, between 2022-05-08 and 2022-05-18. In 2022 loop users therefore appear to have de-risked more than they were liquidated (inference). A deeper depeg is untested. This is one paper.

Kamino prices SOL LSTs by stake rate (SOL staked / LST minted), read from the stake pool account, not by DEX price. A market discount, such as JitoSOL at 0.95 SOL against a 1.05 SOL stake rate, does not change a Multiply position's LTV. A real loss of backing (exploit, slashing) lowers the stake rate and does change it. Kamino says this is why market depegs have not liquidated LST Multiply positions.

Kamino prices Solana LSTs at the stake rate (SOL_staked / LST_minted), read from the on-chain stake pool account, so its docs say a JitoSOL DEX price of 0.95 SOL leaves positions valued at about 1.02 SOL unaffected. Jupiter Lend flash loans carry no fee. Its developer docs say to 'Return the same borrowed amount to Jupiter Lend (no fees)', and its user docs say the Multiply flash loan shows 'Flash Loan Fee: Free' and that Unwind adds no protocol fee and also uses a free flash loan. The user's cost is the swap: the docs state that each Multiply or Unwind swaps tokens through Jupiter, so the user bears price impact and route fees.

A looped position's return on equity is Net = L×Y − (L−1)×B, where L = total collateral ÷ equity, Y = collateral yield and B = borrow rate. The same value is Y + (L−1)×(Y−B). Three write-ups reach it by different routes. Kamino states 'Net APY = (Collateral Yield × Leverage) − (Borrow Rate × (Leverage − 1))'. The arXiv paper maximises Σ xℓs − Σ x(ℓ−1)b over equity x and leverage ℓ and rewrites it as ξs + Σ m·x·(s − b) with m = ℓ−1. SODAX sums the loop series to total supplied 1/(1−LTV) and total borrowed LTV/(1−LTV) and gets supplyRate + leverage × (supplyRate − borrowRate).

A stress simulation of Aave/Lido/Curve leverage staking found that leverage amplifies cascading liquidations. The paper identifies 442 leveraged-staking positions holding 537,123 ETH over 963 days. It states the simulated liquidation reached 497,375 ETH, which it calls 16 times the no-leverage case. This is a simulation under an extreme stETH price path, not an observed event.

Nansen (reported 2022-06-29) concluded that contagion from the UST de-peg and Terra collapse was likely the main driver of the stETH discount. bETH holders redeemed to stETH and sold it for ETH. Inside a group the program also forces the borrow factor to 1.0: Reserve::borrow_factor_f(true) returns Fraction::ONE, and klend-sdk's getMaxAndLiquidationLtvAndBorrowFactorForPair returns borrowFactor 1 for any group. A group therefore overrides three inputs at once (LTV, liquidation threshold, borrow factor) and also caps the liquidation bonus. Outside a group the debt reserve's borrow factor divides borrowing power: Kamino's litepaper gives capacity as collateral amount x LTV / borrow factor.

Kamino's own comparison says manual looping or unwinding across 8-10 transactions exposes the user to price moves between steps and separate slippage on every swap, while atomic Multiply uses a single consolidated slippage check in one block.

Aave's repay-with-collateral adapter takes a flash loan, repays the borrow, pulls the user's collateral, and swaps it to the debt asset to repay the flash loan. Its debt-swap adapter flash-loans a replacement asset, swaps it to the old debt asset, repays that debt and re-borrows. Both route the swap through ParaSwap calldata. The Aave docs name no maxSlippage parameter and give no flash premium rate.

For fixed-rate debt the SDK adds an early-repay penalty to the unwind: it flash-borrows principal plus penalty, repays the principal, and withdraws proportionally more collateral to cover the penalty, rounded flash fees and a full-repayment cushion. A close of a fixed-term Multiply position therefore carries a cost that variable-rate debt does not.

In a Pendle PT loop the same formula applies with Y set to the PT's fixed APY and B usually variable. Notional says total APY depends on 'the PT APY', 'the APY spread (APY spread = PT APY - borrow APY)' and 'the leverage ratio'. Pendle's docs say 'Your realised discount becomes your fixed yield' and that capital and return are guaranteed only 'if you hold until maturity'; an early exit depends on the PT's market price and 'may earn higher or lower (in extreme cases, at a loss) than the advertised APY at entry'. A fixed Y removes yield variance but not borrow-rate or exit-price exposure.

klend refuses to roll over a fixed-term borrow for a position that is in an elevation group (RolloverNotSupportedInElevationGroup: 'Rollover is not supported for obligations in an elevation group'). Kamino docs offer fixed-rate borrowing as a way to lock a Multiply borrow cost, and the SDK defines fixed-rate Multiply obligation types.

Looping comes in three shapes that share the same geometric math. Same-asset recursion supplies and borrows one asset (Spark's example: 100 USDC, borrow 80, re-supply to 180, borrow 64, re-supply to 244). A swap loop supplies A, borrows B, swaps B for A and re-deposits (the Bank of Canada definition, and the shape of LST/underlying loops). A cross-asset re-supply loop borrows a second asset and supplies that instead: in 1inch's July 2026 case a wallet supplied 95.67 WETH and looped about $430K of stablecoin debt and collateral, so its WETH amount never grew.

Three published rules count looping on-chain, and they measure different things. The Bank of Canada flags a borrow of B against A, followed within one day by a swap of B back into A, followed within the next day by a new borrow against that A (an approximation; longer windows gave no significant difference). IFCA rebuilds each address's collateral and debt from deposit, withdraw, borrow and repay flows and computes leverage = C*Pc/(C*Pc - D*Pd). Galaxy uses balance-sheet snapshots: debt-weighted LTV and debt/equity per collateral asset, inverted into an implied loop count. Results from the thr

The formula rearranges to Net = Y + (Y−B)×(L−1): unlevered yield plus the yield spread earned on each borrowed dollar. Kamino writes it as 'Net APY = Collateral Yield + Yield Spread × (Leverage − 1)'. SODAX writes it as effectiveNet = effectiveSupply + leverage × spread, where its 'leverage' is the borrowed amount per unit of deposit (that is, L−1), so the two forms are algebraically identical. Check which convention a calculator uses before comparing numbers.

The formula rearranges to Net = Y + (L−1)×(Y−B): the unlevered yield plus the spread earned on each borrowed unit. Kamino writes 'Collateral Yield + Yield Spread × (Leverage − 1)'; CryptoTicker writes 'result = yield + borrowed units × (yield − borrow rate)'. SODAX writes effectiveNet = effectiveSupply + leverage × spread, but its 'leverage' is debt ÷ equity = targetLTV/(1−targetLTV) = L−1; its code comment says this is 'Not total exposure' and that a UI 'Leverage' label shows 1 + that value. Check whether a calculator's 'leverage' means L or L−1 before comparing numbers.

Aave defines Health Factor = (Total Collateral Value x Weighted Average Liquidation Threshold) / Total Borrow Value; HF below 1 permits liquidation. The liquidation threshold is set per collateral asset by Aave governance. For a single collateral asset whose debt price is fixed, setting HF = 1 and solving gives liquidation price = debt / (collateral amount x liquidation threshold); this rearrangement is derived here, not quoted from Aave. The same bound can be written as a tolerable price drop of 1 - 1/HF.

It re-prices the obligation under the new group and reverts with UnhealthyElevationGroupLtv if the allowed borrow value is below the borrow-factor-adjusted debt. Bank of Canada Staff Analytical Paper 2026-13 (Chiu and Danisman, April 2026) studies Aave V3 and finds many users engage in recursive leverage despite overcollateralization requirements, and that liquidations occur in concentrated waves. The abstract page gives no prevalence percentage.

Stake-rate pricing does not cover fundamental depegs. If a stake-pool exploit drains SOL, the stake rate falls and liquidations proceed normally. Kamino also states the design assumes arbitrageurs buy discounted LSTs and unstake them. If arbitrage fails (for example, a pool bug blocks unstaking), the protocol may hold collateral valued above what the market will pay, and any resulting bad debt is socialized among lenders in that market.

With initial collateral c0 and a flash loan F = k*c0 swapped into collateral, the final borrow B = F must satisfy B/C = k/(k+1) <= L, where C = (k+1)*c0. That gives k <= L/(1 - L) and total collateral c0*(1 + k) <= c0/(1 - L): the same ceiling as the infinite manual loop. Baude et al.'s cap l <= 1/(1 - maxLTV) is the same bound with l = k + 1.

Neither Kamino deleverage guide discusses price impact or liquidity depth; they give only a slippage tolerance in basis points (the example uses 50 bps, with a note that some assets need more) and a quoteBufferBps setting. The user must estimate size-dependent price impact on the collateral-to-debt route, for example from a live quote, before choosing a tolerance.

The quoter must return priceAInB as the mid price (amountOut / amountIn of the best route, each in token units, before slippage). The SDK applies slippagePct itself, so passing a minimum-out price counts slippage twice and mis-sizes the swap. A separate quoteBufferBps setting inflates the input amount used for the quote request; the withdraw example sets it to 0.

Yield-side inputs in calculators may be trailing averages. SODAX takes the LSD staking yield from DefiLlama's latest apy value (a trailing 7-30 day window, per the SODAX doc) and falls back to a hardcoded value flagged stale:true if the fetch fails, so a calculator's Y can lag the live rate.

Kamino states that zero SOL-LST Multiply positions have been liquidated by market price moves, including April 2025 and February 2026. That is a vendor self-report, and a search for an independent counter-example found none. It covers price-driven liquidation only, not a staking-protocol loss or a sustained negative spread.

klend defines ALL_CHECKS as all six price-status flags and LIQUIDATION_CHECKS as only PRICE_LOADED, PRICE_AGE_CHECKED and PRICE_USAGE_ALLOWED (0b00100011). TWAP_CHECKED, TWAP_AGE_CHECKED and HEURISTIC_CHECKED are not required to liquidate, while borrowing needs ALL_CHECKS.

A group's max_liquidation_bonus_bps can only tighten the liquidator bonus. get_emode_max_liquidation_bonus returns the group cap only if it is non-zero and not above either reserve's own max_liquidation_bonus_bps; otherwise it returns u16::MAX, meaning no group cap. The bonus ceiling is min(max(collateral reserve max, debt reserve max), group cap). Kamino's docs describe the group cap as 'tighter than default for correlated assets'.

klend-sdk chooses the group for a deposit-and-borrow pair, which is what Multiply uses. getCommonElevationGroupsForPair keeps a group only if both reserves list it, allow_new_loans is not 0, the collateral reserve's borrow_limit_against_this_collateral_in_elevation_group for that group is above 0, and the group's debt_reserve is the reserve being borrowed. getPreferredElevationGroupForBorrowPair picks the common group with the highest ltv_pct and returns 0 (no eMode) if none qualifies. The Multiply deposit builder requests a group unless the caller passes override 0.

An in-group position can hold at most one borrow, and that borrow must be the group's debt_reserve. Borrowing any other reserve fails with ElevationGroupHasAnotherDebtReserve ('In elevation group attempt to borrow from a reserve that is not the debt reserve').

request_elevation_group works only on a freshly refreshed obligation and only while the market is out of emergency mode. It fails if the position is already in that group, or if the group has allow_new_loans = 0, no debt_reserve, or max_reserves_as_collateral below the position's deposit count. It then reprices the position under the new group and fails with UnhealthyElevationGroupLtv ('The current obligation must have most or all its debt repaid before changing the elevation group') if existing debt exceeds the new allowed borrow value.

Each Multiply position lives in its own obligation of type MultiplyObligation (tag 1), whose PDA seeds are the collateral mint and the debt mint. A normal borrow uses VanillaObligation (tag 0) with default seeds, and fixed-rate Multiply uses tag 4 seeded by reserve addresses. A Multiply position is therefore keyed to one collateral/debt pair, which fits a group's single-debt-reserve rule.

Groups are written through the owner-gated update_lending_market instruction (mode UpdateElevationGroup), exposed by klend-sdk (KaminoManager.updateLendingMarketIxs) and the Kamino CLI (kamino-manager update-lending-market-from-config). Each participating reserve must separately list the group id in config.elevation_groups (update-reserve-config). Kamino's docs say elevation-group configuration is not available through the REST API, which serves read access only.

A reserve joins groups through ReserveConfig.elevation_groups, an array of up to 20 group ids. A position (obligation) is in at most one group at a time (obligation.elevation_group, one u8). The owner switches groups with the request_elevation_group instruction, whose only argument is the target group id. Id 0 leaves eMode, and the SDK sends id 0 after a full repay of a single-debt position.
